title: Every Forecaster Is Saying the Same Thing: India Is Slowing Down. Here Is Why.
excerpt: S&P, UBS, HDFC Bank, and the RBI all project growth between 6.2% and 6.7% for FY27 — down from 7.7% — as energy stress, a record monsoon deficit, and softening business confidence converge on the world's fastest-growing major economy.
body:
Every major forecaster to weigh in this week has said the same thing: India's economy is slowing down, and there is not much the government can do about it in the short term.

S&P Global Ratings set the headline number on Wednesday, projecting real GDP growth of 6.6% for the fiscal year ending March 2027 — a sharp drop from the 7.7% India posted in FY26 and the 7.1% in FY25. The Reserve Bank of India, which had already cut its own forecast to 6.6% earlier this month, is now in agreement. HDFC Bank is marginally more optimistic at 6.7%. UBS, the Swiss investment bank, is the most bearish of the lot at 6.2%.

The numbers all point in one direction: growth is decelerating, and the causes are piling up.

## The Oil Squeeze

India imports 88% of its crude oil. That single fact makes it structurally vulnerable to energy shocks, and the West Asia conflict has delivered exactly that. Brent crude futures are currently trading around $77 a barrel — well below the $126 peak touched during the worst of the Iran war — but still elevated enough to keep India's import bill uncomfortably high.

S&P described the energy stress as "visible," noting that Indian industry faces a "substantial rise in input costs and suppliers' delivery time." Higher energy costs feed directly into manufacturing margins, transportation costs, and ultimately consumer prices. India has already raised administered prices for petrol, diesel, and cooking gas in recent months.

The net effect on inflation is significant. S&P projects consumer inflation will climb to 5.1% this fiscal year, a level that could force the Reserve Bank to hike interest rates in the second half of FY27 — a reversal after months of easing that had buoyed markets and borrowers alike.

## The Monsoon Gap

El Niño is back, and the monsoon is paying the price. India's cumulative rainfall deficit stood at 43% as of June 22, the widest gap in over a decade. The India Meteorological Department has lowered its monsoon forecast to 90% of the long-period average, the weakest first estimate in 26 years. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration assigns a 67% probability to a "Super El Niño" this year — the strongest ever recorded.

This matters because agriculture still accounts for 16% of India's GDP and employs 45% of its workforce. A weak monsoon means lower crop yields, higher food prices, and reduced rural demand — the last of which hits consumer goods companies, two-wheeler manufacturers, and FMCG firms that depend on India's vast hinterland for volume.

The government has drawn up contingency plans for 315 districts, recommending alternative crops suited to low-rainfall conditions. But crop-switching takes time, and the damage to planting schedules may already be done.

## The PMI Slowdown

India's private sector expanded at its slowest pace in three months in June. HSBC's flash Composite PMI fell to 57.4 from 59.3 in May. Services activity dropped to a 17-month low of 57.3. Manufacturing slipped to 54.5.

The data is still in expansion territory — anything above 50 signals growth — but the direction is concerning. New orders, the best proxy for demand, rose at their slowest pace since March. Firms cited competitive pressures and gas shortages as headwinds.

Job creation is weakening too. Employment across the private sector grew only marginally in June, the weakest gain in six months. Hiring at both factories and service providers hit its lowest level since December.

Business confidence has fallen below its long-run average, with manufacturers reporting sentiment at its weakest in nearly four years.

## What It Means for NRI Investors

For non-resident Indians with money parked in Indian markets, the picture is mixed. The Nifty and Sensex gained over 4% in the seven sessions before the PMI data hit, buoyed by falling oil prices and easing foreign outflows. But the rally triggered profit-booking once the soft economic numbers came through.

IT stocks, a bellwether for the diaspora, fell 2.2% after Jefferies and Morgan Stanley flagged soft demand following Accenture's weak outlook. Rising expectations of a US Federal Reserve rate hike added pressure, given the risk to client spending.

The rupee is weakening, which cuts both ways. NRIs sending money home get more rupees per dollar, but equity returns denominated in dollars take a hit. S&P noted that authorities have taken measures to encourage foreign capital inflows, but the current account deficit is rising.

For those holding Indian bonds or mutual funds, the prospect of an RBI rate hike could provide better yields on new fixed-income investments — but it would also mean existing bond portfolios lose value. FCNR(B) deposits, which the RBI recently sweetened for NRIs, remain one of the more attractive parking spots for dollar savings.

## The Bigger Picture

India at 6.6% growth is still the fastest-growing major economy in the world. China's post-Covid recovery has stalled well below that level. But the story of the last two years has been India outperforming its own trajectory — 7.7% was not supposed to be the norm, but it started to feel like it.

The correction to 6.6% is a reminder that India's growth engine runs on two fuels that it does not fully control: imported oil and monsoon rain. When both are working against it, even strong fundamentals — domestic demand, a young workforce, digital infrastructure — can only do so much.
